transcript:
Section 1: The Library Book Club Mix-Up

Mia: Hi, Tom. Thanks for meeting me here at the community library. I thought we could finalize the plan for next month's book club.
Tom: Sure, Mia. But first, I have to admit something. I think I mixed up the dates for our reading challenge.
Mia: What do you mean?
Tom: Well, I told everyone the challenge starts on the fifth of March, but the library newsletter says it begins on the fifteenth.
Mia: Oh no. That's a big difference. We need to fix that quickly.
Tom: I know. I've already sent a correction email to all members. But some people might not check their inbox.
Mia: Right. We should also put a notice on the library's main door.
Tom: Good idea. I'll print it this afternoon. Now, about the book selection. You suggested we read a mystery novel, but I was thinking of something shorter.
Mia: Shorter? But our members enjoy long stories.
Tom: True, but for a timed reading exercise, a shorter book might be better. We want them to finish within the session.
Mia: Hmm. You have a point. But the theme for week 42 is 'timed reading: matching, gap-fill, and long-text stamina'. A long text would actually help them practice stamina.
Tom: That's a fair argument. Okay, let's go with a long novel, but we'll break it into sections.
Mia: Perfect. And for the grammar focus, we need to highlight pronouns, parts of speech, and parallel structure.
Tom: Yes, and also long sentence breakdown. I can prepare a handout on that.
Mia: Great. By the way, did you confirm the room booking?
Tom: I did. We have the meeting room from 6 to 8 p.m. on the twentieth.
Mia: The twentieth? But that's a Tuesday. Our usual day is Thursday.
Tom: Oh, you're right. I booked the wrong day. Let me call the library office to change it.
Mia: Thanks. While you do that, I'll draft the reading questions.
Tom: Sounds good. Also, should we provide refreshments?
Mia: The library allows light snacks, but no hot drinks.
Tom: Got it. I'll bring some biscuits and juice.
Mia: And don't forget to mention the new starting date in the reminder email.
Tom: I will. I'll send it tomorrow morning.
Mia: One more thing: the sign-up sheet. We need to cap the group at fifteen people.
Tom: Fifteen? Last time we had twenty.
Mia: I know, but the meeting room only has fifteen chairs.
Tom: Okay, fifteen it is. I'll update the online form.
Mia: Great. So, to summarize: the challenge starts on the fifteenth, we're reading a long novel in sections, the room is booked for Thursday the twentieth from 6 to 8, and we'll cap at fifteen.
Tom: That's correct. And I'll handle the notice, the room change, and the reminder email.
Mia: Perfect. Thanks, Tom. See you soon.

Section 2: Community Garden Project: A Talk by the Coordinator

Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to this information session about the Green Roots Community Garden project. My name is Sarah, and I’m the volunteer coordinator for the project. I’d like to tell you about our plans for the coming year and how you can get involved.

First, a bit of background. The garden is located on the old railway land behind the library on Mill Street. We started three years ago with just eight raised beds, and now we have twenty-four. The land is owned by the city council, but we manage it as a community group. We have a small committee of five people who make decisions about the garden.

Now, let me explain the membership system. Anyone can join for a small annual fee. For an individual, it’s fifteen pounds per year. For a family, it’s twenty-five pounds. This money goes towards seeds, tools, and water. Members get their own small plot to grow vegetables or flowers. If you don’t want a plot, you can still become a ‘friend’ of the garden for five pounds a year, and you can help with events and general maintenance.

We also run regular workshops. These are usually on Saturday mornings from ten to twelve. The next one is on the first Saturday of next month, and it’s about growing tomatoes. You don’t need to book for workshops; just turn up. But for the bigger events, like our summer fair, we do need volunteers to sign up in advance.

One important thing: the garden is open to the public every day from sunrise to sunset, but the tool shed is only open when a committee member is present, usually on Wednesday and Sunday afternoons. So if you need to borrow a spade or a watering can, come on those days.

We also have a children’s area with a small playhouse and a sandpit. Children must be accompanied by an adult at all times. We ask that you don’t bring dogs into the garden, except guide dogs.

Finally, if you’d like to join, you can pick up a form from the library or download one from our website. The website address is on the leaflet I’m holding up. You can also email us, but please don’t phone the library—they’re busy enough! Our email is on the leaflet too.

Thank you for listening. I hope to see you in the garden soon.

Section 3: Week 42 Listening: The Campus Library Redesign Project

TUTOR: Good morning, Mia and Leo. Thanks for coming. Let's review your proposals for the library redesign. Mia, you wanted to start with the reading rooms, is that right?
MIA: Yes, but actually I've changed my mind. I now think the group study rooms are more urgent. The reading rooms are fine, but students keep complaining they can't book a group room.
LEO: I agree with Mia. The group rooms are always full. But I also think we shouldn't ignore the silent study area. Some students need complete quiet.
TUTOR: Good point, Leo. So we have three areas: group study, silent study, and the reading rooms. Let's prioritise. Mia, you said group study first. Why?
MIA: Because the demand is highest. In the survey, 70 percent of students said they had trouble finding a group room. Only 20 percent mentioned the reading rooms.
TUTOR: That's a strong argument. Leo, you mentioned the silent area. What's your evidence?
LEO: Well, the silent area is often noisy because it's next to the café. Students say they can hear the coffee machine. So maybe we should move the silent area to the second floor.
TUTOR: Moving it could be expensive. But let's note it. Now, what about the furniture? I saw your sketches.
MIA: We suggest flexible furniture for the group rooms—tables on wheels and chairs that can be moved easily. That way, the rooms can be used for different group sizes.
LEO: And for the silent area, we recommend individual desks with screens, so students can't see each other and get distracted.
TUTOR: I like both ideas. But have you considered the budget? The library has a limited budget this year.
MIA: Yes, we have. We think the flexible furniture is cheaper than fixed furniture because it lasts longer and needs less repair.
LEO: Actually, I'm not sure about that. Fixed furniture might be more durable. But flexible furniture is more popular with students.
TUTOR: Let's check the prices later. Now, what about the reading rooms? You haven't said much about them.
MIA: We suggest adding more power sockets and better lighting. Students often study there with laptops, and the sockets are insufficient.
LEO: And the lighting is too dim in the evening. Several students said they get headaches.
TUTOR: Good. So your priorities are: group study rooms first, then silent area, then reading rooms. Is that correct?
MIA: Yes, that's right.
LEO: Actually, I'd put the silent area second, but the reading rooms are definitely last.
TUTOR: Fine. Now, let's talk about the timeline. When do you plan to present your final proposal?
MIA: We plan to present it at the end of next month, after we get the cost estimates.
TUTOR: That gives you about four weeks. Make sure you include a clear budget table. Also, consider consulting the student union for feedback.
LEO: We will. We've already scheduled a meeting with them next week.
TUTOR: Excellent. One more thing: the library director wants a one-page summary. Can you prepare that?
MIA: Yes, we can. We'll send it to you by Friday.
TUTOR: Perfect. I look forward to reading it. Keep up the good work.

Section 4: The Science of Reading: How We Process Text Under Time Pressure

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about the science of reading, especially how we process text when we are under time pressure. This is relevant for students who need to read quickly in exams or at work. Let me start with a key idea: reading is not a single skill but a set of processes that work together. When we read, our eyes move in small jumps called saccades, and we fixate on words for about 200 to 250 milliseconds. During fixation, we recognize words and access their meaning. But we don't read every word equally; we skip short, common words like 'the' or 'and' more often. This is because our brain predicts what comes next based on context. However, prediction is not always accurate, so we also need to check back. This brings me to the first main point: skimming and scanning are different strategies. Skimming means reading quickly to get the general idea, while scanning means looking for specific information, like a date or a name. Skimming is useful for getting an overview, but scanning is better when you need to find a particular fact. Now, let me move to the second point: the role of working memory. Working memory is the part of your mind that holds information temporarily while you process it. When you read a long sentence, you need to keep the beginning in mind until you reach the end. If the sentence is complex, your working memory can become overloaded, and you may need to re-read. This is why long texts can be tiring. To manage this, good readers break long sentences into smaller chunks. They also use strategies like underlining or taking notes. Next, I want to discuss grammar and reading. Specifically, understanding pronoun reference is crucial. For example, in the sentence 'The scientist studied the data because she wanted to test her hypothesis,' the pronoun 'she' refers to 'the scientist.' If you misidentify the referent, you may misunderstand the whole sentence. Similarly, parallel structure can help you predict what comes next. For instance, in a list like 'reading, writing, and speaking,' the parallel form signals that another skill is coming. Finally, let me address the issue of time pressure. Research shows that when people are given a time limit, they tend to focus on the main ideas and skip details. This can be efficient, but it can also lead to errors. A better approach is to practice timed reading regularly, gradually increasing the difficulty. In conclusion, reading under time pressure requires a balance of speed and accuracy. By understanding how your eyes move, how your memory works, and how grammar helps, you can become a more effective reader. Thank you for listening.

grammar.title: 指代、词性与平行结构；长句拆解
grammar.explanation: 指代（pronouns）用来代替名词，如he、she、it、they。词性（parts of speech）包括名词、动词、形容词等。平行结构（parallel structure）指用相同语法形式连接并列成分，如“matching, gap-fill, and long-text stamina”都是名词短语。长句拆解（long sentence breakdown）是把长句分成主句和从句，找出核心意思。
grammar.example: the theme for week 42 is 'timed reading: matching, gap-fill, and long-text stamina'
